outcome: No progress found: the problem remains exactly as stated, with the only three known strongly regular geodetic graphs still C5, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman-Singleton graph (all Moore graphs), and no proof or disproof of infinitude or of the existence of a non-Moore example.
summary: This bullet asks whether there exist infinitely many strongly regular geodetic graphs, or any strongly regular geodetic graph that is not a Moore graph (a strongly regular geodetic graph necessarily has mu=1, and is a Moore graph exactly when lambda=0; the three currently known examples — C5, the Petersen graph, and the Hoffman–Singleton graph — are all Moore graphs). The current Wikipedia 'Geodetic graph' article states plainly: 'Despite additional research on the properties such a graph must have, it is not known whether there are more of these graphs, or infinitely many of these graphs,' confirming the problem is still open as of today. The most relevant piece of research activity in the window is Cornelsen, Pfretzschner and Stumpf's 'Geodetic Graphs: Experiments and New Constructions' (arXiv:2308.08970), first posted 17 August 2023 (before the frozen revision, so not itself a window event) but revised 27 January 2025 (a minor correction changing a vertex count from 32 to 33, not touching the strongly-regular question). That paper's exhaustive computer search establishes that there are no regular geodetic graphs beyond the known list (odd cycles, complete graphs, the Petersen graph, the Hoffman-Singleton graph, and one 28-vertex cubic graph) up to 32 vertices, and it exhibits two new infinite families of geodetic graphs, but none of those new families are strongly regular — they are stated by the authors to be regular but not strongly regular, so they do not bear on this bullet's question. A second paper in the area, Elder, Piggott, Stober, Thumm and Weiß, 'Finite Groups with Geodetic Cayley Graphs' (arXiv:2406.00261, submitted 1 June 2024, published in Experimental Mathematics 2025), addresses a different, narrower question — geodetic Cayley graphs of finite groups — and conjectures that odd cycles and complete graphs are the only such graphs; this is a related problem (restricted to the Cayley-graph setting) rather than a case of the stated bullet, since it is not restricted to strongly regular graphs and does not settle anything about non-Cayley strongly regular geodetic graphs. No paper, preprint, blog post, or database entry found in the 26 January 2024 to present window reports a new strongly regular geodetic graph, a proof of infinitude, or a proof of finiteness. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2308.08970 paper's January 2025 revision counts as a window event worth flagging even though it made no substantive change relevant to this bullet; I include it in status_sources/summary for completeness but it does not change the status from open, since the correction was to a vertex count for a different (non-strongly-regular) enumeration result.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of infinitude of strongly regular geodetic graphs, or the discovery/construction of a single new strongly regular geodetic graph with lambda>0 (hence not a Moore graph), or a proof that no such graph exists beyond the Moore graphs.
